Is MFA required or optional, and per-tenant configurable? What are session lifetime, idle timeout, and revocation semantics (does an admin-initiated revocation kill live sessions immediately, cf. AR-08)? What CSRF strategy applies to the browser UI, and what rate limits protect authentication, the public share-link endpoints (AR-13), and the webhook-configuration endpoints (AR-12)? Are long-lived API tokens for programmatic access in scope, and how are they scoped and revoked?
impact: Enterprise SSO with directory-driven deprovisioning is a materially larger deliverable than local accounts, and it is the usual expectation for a multi-tenant B2B approval product — the answer changes the phase count.
Session revocation latency is the same class of decision as cache-based permission staleness (AR-08) and must be consistent with it, or a revoked user retains access by a different route.
Unauthenticated share-link endpoints without rate limiting are directly brute-forceable against the token space in AR-13.
The mandatory security tests in the coding standards (input validation, authz, injection, rate limiting) cannot be specified until the auth model exists.

material_ambiguities.question: What is the compliance and data-protection envelope, supplied by an accountable owner rather than inferred? Which regimes apply (GDPR, UK GDPR, CCPA, SOC 2, HIPAA, sector-specific rules)? Are there data-residency constraints on where documents, personal data, and audit records may be stored and processed, including by the email and webhook delivery paths? What are the retention and erasure obligations, and how do they reconcile with an append-only audit log (AR-15) and stored document versions (AR-16)? Does an approval in this system carry legal or e-signature weight — which would add identity-assurance, intent-capture, and evidence-package requirements to AR-04?
impact: Data residency can forbid a single global datastore and a single delivery region, constraining the deployment topology before any code is planned.
E-signature weight, if required, adds signer-identity assurance and a tamper-evident evidence package to every approval — a requirement area that is entirely absent from the current scope.
Erasure obligations interact irreconcilably with immutable audit and document versioning unless a strategy is designed up front; retrofitting one means rewriting the storage model.
This class of requirement must come from a qualified owner: a plan built on assumed regulatory scope is both wrong and unsafe, and no auto-design delegation may resolve it.

material_ambiguities.question: Is this greenfield or an extension of an existing system, and what is the v1 scope boundary? If an existing system: what are the current schema, API surface, client application, identity provider, and queue technology, and which clients must keep working? Which of the eight stated capabilities ship in the first release — specifically, are webhooks, external URL sharing, and the background extraction job all in v1, or do some follow? What is explicitly out of scope (approval templates, delegation and out-of-office, bulk actions, e-signature, mobile apps, document editing, search)?
impact: No repository or existing code was supplied, so every technical recommendation for this system is currently ungrounded and cannot cite real code as the working standards require.
Brownfield status determines whether a migration and backfill workstream exists at all and whether API versioning is mandatory (AR-17).
Webhooks and external sharing are each large enough to be their own requirement document with their own security surface; deferring either materially changes the plan's size and sequencing.
Without a stated out-of-scope list, the "Won't Have" sections cannot be written and scope leak between requirement documents is unpreventable.

material_ambiguities.question: Define the terms the brief uses inconsistently or without definition: "organization" vs. "team" vs. "tenant" vs. "workspace"; "approve" vs. "sign off"; "request changes" vs. "reject"; "document" vs. "version" vs. "submission"; "reviewer" vs. "approver" vs. "assignee"; "administrator" (team-level or organization-level or platform-level); "important action"; "usable" during a deployment; "external collaborator" vs. "guest" vs. "user"; and "pending".
impact: Each of these currently denotes two or more operationally distinct things, so requirements written on them are ambiguous by construction and will be implemented inconsistently across the API, the UI, the webhook payloads, and the audit log.
"Organization" and "team" are used in adjacent sentences to scope two different permissions; until they are distinguished, AR-01 and AR-03 cannot both be answered coherently.
These terms become API field names, event type names, database columns, and customer-facing text, where renaming later is a breaking change to the webhook contract (AR-11).
"Important action" is the entire scope of the audit requirement; leaving it undefined makes AR-15 unverifiable.

material_ambiguities.question: What are the non-functional targets? Expected and peak counts of organizations, users per organization, documents per organization, and documents per list view; the latency budget for the document list (which is the only thing that can justify the five-minute cache); the end-to-end SLA for metadata extraction and for notification and webhook delivery; the availability target and error budget; deployment frequency; and maximum document size and total storage per tenant.
impact: The five-minute cache is presently a solution with no stated problem — without a latency target and a data-volume figure, its necessity and its TTL cannot be evaluated against AR-07 and AR-18.
Volume figures determine whether the list path needs pagination, indexing strategy, and denormalization, but not the overall architecture, so the plan can be structured before they land.

Can be carried as an explicit stated assumption (interactive list under 300ms, extraction within seconds, moderate per-tenant volumes) and corrected before implementation without invalidating the plan's phase structure.
Sets the performance acceptance criteria for the mandatory non-functional requirement document.

material_ambiguities.question: What verification bar defines done? Which test classes are mandatory — a cross-tenant isolation suite, a full authorization-matrix suite derived from AR-02, concurrency interleavings (simultaneous conflicting decisions, admin override racing a reviewer, optimistic retry duplicates, decision against a superseded version), stale-cache-after-revocation assertions, webhook signature and SSRF tests, malicious-upload tests, and a mixed-version rolling-deploy test? Is an end-to-end suite against a real browser in scope, and is there a required coverage or break-rate threshold?
impact: Without a named bar the plan has no oracle for its security and concurrency requirements, and "done" is unfalsifiable.

A sound default set already exists in the project's testing standards and the selected domains' required-interleavings lists, so this can be proposed as a stated assumption without changing the architecture.
Determines whether a multi-tenant test fixture and a deploy-simulation harness are built as deliverables rather than assumed.
The specification-versus-implementation test split means the authorization matrix (AR-02) must be expressible as spec tests, which constrains how it is documented.

material_ambiguities.question: What is the user-facing surface for failure and edge states? What is shown when an optimistic action is rolled back, when a decision conflicts (AR-05), when a share link is expired or revoked, when metadata extraction failed, when a list is empty or a user has no permission, and when the service is mid-deployment? Are accessibility conformance (e.g. WCAG level) and internationalization or localization in scope, and which locales and timezone display rules apply?
impact: Error text for a rolled-back optimistic action is the only signal a user gets that their action did not happen; its absence is a correctness problem disguised as a copy gap.
An expired share link's page reveals or conceals the document's existence to an unauthenticated visitor — an information-disclosure choice, though a narrow one.
Accessibility conformance level and locale set affect component choices and content pipeline but not the domain model, so the plan can proceed under a stated assumption.
Timezone display rules must agree with the audit log's stored timestamps (AR-15) or the two disagree in support conversations.
